topic.title: Education: Origins and daily operation in Community Learning Centres
topic.focus: how the initiative began and how it works each day

candidate_instructions: Read all five sections. Answer Questions 1-25. Follow the stated word limits exactly.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Community Learning Centres started ten years ago in the city of Leicester. Local people wanted a place where residents could learn new skills for free. The first centre opened in an old church building. Local businesses donated tables, chairs, and computers. Volunteers offered their time to teach classes. Today, there are five centres across the city helping thousands of residents.

sections.heading: How it operates
sections.text: Each centre opens five days a week from 10 am to 5 pm. Classes are offered in English, maths, computer skills, and job training. Students can attend classes for as long as they need. Most courses are free, although some special courses cost a small amount. Teachers are both paid professionals and volunteers from the community. The centres also provide lunch at low prices to help students stay healthy.

sections.heading: Evidence and experience
sections.text: Since the centres opened, over 15,000 people have attended courses. Many students have found jobs after completing their training. Some moved to better positions in their companies. Others started their own small businesses. Student feedback shows that 92% of people feel more confident after their courses. Teachers report that students often make new friends and feel more connected to their communities.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: The centres face several challenges. Funding is limited, so they cannot always hire enough teachers. Some buildings are old and need repairs. In winter, heating costs are high. Transport to the centres can be difficult for students who live far away. The centres need more equipment for computer classes. Despite these problems, demand continues to grow every year.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: The charity plans to open two new centres in the next three years. They want to offer more online courses for people who cannot attend classes in person. New partnerships with local employers will help create more job opportunities. The centres will expand evening classes for working people. A recent government grant will help pay for new computers and teaching materials. Leaders believe these changes will help even more residents develop new skills and improve their lives.

passage.full_text:
Paragraph 1 — Background
Community Learning Centres started ten years ago in the city of Leicester. Local people wanted a place where residents could learn new skills for free. The first centre opened in an old church building. Local businesses donated tables, chairs, and computers. Volunteers offered their time to teach classes. Today, there are five centres across the city helping thousands of residents.

Paragraph 2 — How it operates
Each centre opens five days a week from 10 am to 5 pm. Classes are offered in English, maths, computer skills, and job training. Students can attend classes for as long as they need. Most courses are free, although some special courses cost a small amount. Teachers are both paid professionals and volunteers from the community. The centres also provide lunch at low prices to help students stay healthy.

Paragraph 3 — Evidence and experience
Since the centres opened, over 15,000 people have attended courses. Many students have found jobs after completing their training. Some moved to better positions in their companies. Others started their own small businesses. Student feedback shows that 92% of people feel more confident after their courses. Teachers report that students often make new friends and feel more connected to their communities.

Paragraph 4 — Challenges
The centres face several challenges. Funding is limited, so they cannot always hire enough teachers. Some buildings are old and need repairs. In winter, heating costs are high. Transport to the centres can be difficult for students who live far away. The centres need more equipment for computer classes. Despite these problems, demand continues to grow every year.

Paragraph 5 — Next steps
The charity plans to open two new centres in the next three years. They want to offer more online courses for people who cannot attend classes in person. New partnerships with local employers will help create more job opportunities. The centres will expand evening classes for working people. A recent government grant will help pay for new computers and teaching materials. Leaders believe these changes will help even more residents develop new skills and improve their lives.
